challenge: short-term acute heat stress assay: 26 to 35 C over 3 h, 3 h hold at 35 C, return to 26 C over 2 h (repeated 2-3 times depending on species)
persistence_days: 0 (challenge immediately after preconditioning); recovery assessed to 30 d post-challenge
readouts: photosynthetic efficiency; bleaching intensity / tissue colour; survival; recovery trajectory over 30 days
effect_magnitude: stress-hardening succeeded in ALL preconditioned corals; preconditioning reduced the heat stress response by up to 90%, with variable-high slightly outperforming stable-high; in the two highest-survival species all ST and VT fragments survived while ambient-group survival was only 50% and 75%; ambient-preconditioned fragments of one species had not recovered photosynthetic efficiency or tissue colour within 30 days (p<0.05) whereas VT fragments fully recovered (p>0.05); BUT both high-temperature regimes significantly lowered baseline photosynthetic efficiency and/or tissue colour in 4 of 6 species
replication: 432 fragments total; 4-8 colonies per species, each cut into 12 fragments; per run 144 fragments across 12 tanks (6 heat, 6 control), 12 fragments per tank, 3 fragments per colony per tank; sample sizes per species n=8-16; three consecutive runs of two species each
notes: Most systematic multi-species stress-hardening trial available and the strongest evidence that a VARIABLE regime beats a stable one at equal mean. Critical TRADE-OFF documented: preconditioning itself degraded baseline physiology (tissue paling, lower photosynthetic efficiency) exclusively in the branching species, so the intervention has a cost even when it works. Species differed markedly in receptiveness, and species with high inherent tolerance recovered better - authors conclude low-tolerance, low-receptiveness species are poor candidates for this intervention. Persistence of the acquired tolerance itself (i.e. a gap between preconditioning and challenge) was NOT tested; the 30 days is post-challenge recovery.

stressor: elevated temperature (sublethal thermal preconditioning)
dose_treatment: preconditioning 28 C (+3 C above the 25 C control; ramped +1 C/day) vs non-preconditioned and vs control held at 25 C throughout; acute stress 32 C (+8 C, the experimentally determined bleaching threshold)
duration: 7 d at 28 C, then -1 C/day back to 25 C and 5 d at 25 C, then +1 C/day to 32 C held 10 d
challenge: acute stress at 32 C (bleaching threshold) held for 10 days
persistence_days: ~8 (3 d down-ramp plus 5 d at 25 C between the end of preconditioning and the start of the challenge ramp)
readouts: visual bleaching onset; chlorophyll a and c2; Symbiodiniaceae density; antioxidant enzyme activities; lipid peroxidation (LPO); Hsp70 protein; hsp70 gene expression
effect_magnitude: non-preconditioned P. damicornis showed bleaching as early as Day 1 of acute stress whereas preconditioned nubbins showed no signs until Day 10; preconditioned corals maintained chlorophyll a and c2 and Symbiodiniaceae density longer, had higher antioxidant enzyme activity and lower LPO damage, and showed slower Hsp70 down-regulation / sustained Hsp70 above basal levels with delayed or reduced hsp70 transcription
replication: 8 nubbins per treatment group; duplicate aquaria per treatment (control, preconditioned, non-preconditioned); 4 sampling timepoints
notes: One of very few coral studies with a real gap (about 8 days at ambient) between the end of preconditioning and the challenge, and protection was still present - so the induced state survived at least a week. Coded as Decayed because protection was ultimately transient: preconditioned nubbins did bleach by Day 10 of sustained challenge, and necrosis appeared at Day 10 in both preconditioned and non-preconditioned corals. Preconditioning temperature (+3 C) was chosen following Majerova et al. 2021. Authors note no gene expression changes were detected during the preconditioning phase itself, consistent with Bay & Palumbi 2015, and suggest their 3-day recovery sampling may have missed the transient induction.

stressor: elevated temperature (sublethal thermal preconditioning)
dose_treatment: preconditioning 28 C (+3 C above the 25 C control; ramped +1 C/day) vs non-preconditioned and vs control held at 25 C throughout; acute stress 32 C (+8 C, the experimentally determined bleaching threshold)
duration: 7 d at 28 C, then -1 C/day back to 25 C and 5 d at 25 C, then +1 C/day to 32 C held 10 d
challenge: acute stress at 32 C (bleaching threshold) held for 10 days
persistence_days: ~8 (3 d down-ramp plus 5 d at 25 C between the end of preconditioning and the start of the challenge ramp)
readouts: visual bleaching onset; chlorophyll a and c2; Symbiodiniaceae density; antioxidant enzyme activities; lipid peroxidation (LPO); Hsp70 protein; hsp70 gene expression
effect_magnitude: non-preconditioned S. pistillata bleached at Day 3 of acute stress whereas preconditioned nubbins did not bleach until Day 10; preconditioned corals maintained chlorophyll and symbiont density longer with higher antioxidant activity and lower LPO; the acquired thermal tolerance lasted a SHORTER time in S. pistillata than in P. damicornis
replication: 8 nubbins per treatment group; duplicate aquaria per treatment; 4 sampling timepoints
notes: Separate row from the congeneric P. damicornis experiment because the paper's headline conclusion is a SPECIES-SPECIFIC difference in how long the acquired tolerance lasts (shorter in S. pistillata), which is exactly the persistence question the atlas targets. Same caveat: only one gap length was tested, so decay of the gap itself was not resolved - what was observed is decay of protection under sustained challenge.

stressor: elevated temperature applied as a diel-variable (thermally fluctuating) preconditioning regime
dose_treatment: variable treatment: temperature raised from 28 C baseline to 31 C over 3 h, held at 31 C for 3 h, then returned to 28 C, TWICE PER DAY, vs stable 28 C control (baseline 28 C chosen as the average in situ temperature; 31 C selected as sublethal based on prior preconditioning studies)
duration: 28 d of twice-daily variability (after 30 d acclimation at 24 C and a 0.5 C/day ramp to 28 C)
challenge: rapid heat-stress assay applied immediately after the ex situ treatment
readouts: host and Symbiodiniaceae gene expression (RNA-seq); thermal tolerance from the rapid heat-stress assay
effect_magnitude: species-specific responses: A. cervicornis had a much greater transcriptional response than P. clivosa (583 vs 55 differentially expressed genes); in A. cervicornis key stress-response genes were significantly DOWN-regulated (peroxidases, nitric-oxide synthase, tumour necrosis factors) alongside UP-regulation of genes involved in histone modifications
replication: 146-149 fragments per species (5 cm fragments); 8 x 90 L aquaria (4 variable, 4 control); fragments from each colony evenly distributed across tanks
notes: Directly targets assisted acclimatization for Florida restoration priority species using temperature VARIABILITY rather than a static offset. Two findings a lab should note: (1) receptiveness is strongly species-specific (10-fold difference in DEG count between the two species), and (2) up-regulation of HISTONE MODIFICATION genes during preconditioning is one of the few chromatin-level hints in the coral priming literature, worth following up with direct chromatin assays. Authors caution against scaling up before more species are tested.

stressor: elevated temperature (acute sub-bleaching heat priming)
dose_treatment: priming at 32 C (+5 C above the 27 C regional maximum monthly mean) vs naive (no priming) vs control held at 27 C for the whole 5-day experiment; challenge at 33 C (+6 C above MMM); bleaching for these corals occurs at 34 C
duration: priming applied as a single acute exposure (ramp 3 h up, 3 h hold, 2 h down; ~24 h total exposure window), 8 h at temperature
challenge: thermal challenge at 33 C (+6 C above MMM) for 8 h, followed by 16-24 h recovery at 27 C
persistence_days: 2 (preconditioned corals held at control temperature for 48 h between priming and challenge)
readouts: differentially expressed genes and expression intensity (host and symbiont RNA-seq); Fv/Fm; Coral Health Chart colour score and pigment analysis
effect_magnitude: primed corals showed a dampened stress response versus naive corals: a 28% decline in differentially expressed genes and an overall reduction in expression intensity relative to controls; symbionts showed the same dampening; both groups returned to baseline expression after a 16 h recovery at 27 C; no detectable decline in photosynthetic performance or visible physiological stress in either treatment
replication: 10 genotypes across 2 experimental blocks (5 colonies per block); 9 flow-through tanks per block (3x3x3 design, 3 replicates per temperature combination); 5 fragments per tank; 90 RNA samples; 120 fragments photographed for pigment scoring; 3 sampling timepoints (0 h, 6 h, 24 h)
notes: Cleanest short-window persistence measurement in the set: a single acute prime, a defined 48 h gap at control temperature, then a quantified 28% reduction in the transcriptional stress response. Molecular-only benefit - no physiological difference was detectable because neither treatment bleached, so the row documents transcriptional dampening rather than a performance gain. All colonies confirmed by SNP clustering to belong to a single cryptic lineage of Acropora cf. tenuis (Ningaloo Reef, Bundegi Reef), removing cryptic-species confounding.

stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic); heat-killed Vibrio splendidus as a comparison elicitor
dose_treatment: 240 ug poly(I:C) per oyster by intramuscular injection vs sterile seawater injection
duration: single injection, 1 d before challenge
challenge: OsHV-1 uvar injection challenge
readouts: proportion of virus-infected oysters at 48 h post-infection; immune gene expression (TLR, MyD88, IRF, PKR)
effect_magnitude: 11% of poly(I:C)-primed oysters OsHV-1-positive at 48 h post-infection vs 100% of seawater controls; priming with heat-killed V. splendidus gave no protection
replication: not reported
notes: Foundational paper establishing the poly(I:C) antiviral state in C. gigas; effect measured as infection prevalence not survival; specificity shown by failure of a bacterial elicitor to protect against virus

stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: not reported (poly(I:C) injected into parents; dose not stated in the retrievable text; de Kantzow et al. 2023 lists 250 and 500 ug per oyster as doses used across this literature)
duration: single parental injection before spawning
challenge: OsHV-1 exposure of F1 D-veliger larvae
readouts: F1 larval survival to OsHV-1; IRF2 mRNA in larvae; parental survival
effect_magnitude: Offspring of poly(I:C)-treated parents had double the chance of surviving OsHV-1 exposure vs controls; larval mortality at 96 h post-exposure halved relative to seawater-treated broodstock (as restated by de Kantzow et al. 2023); IRF2 mRNA elevated in larvae
replication: not reported
notes: The foundational transgenerational immune priming (TGEP) paper; authors note poly(I:C) did not affect parental survival so the offspring effect cannot be genetic selection, and propose epigenetic reprogramming or maternal provisioning - but no methylation or chromatin assay was performed

stressor: poly(I:C) HMW (1.5-8 kb); also poly(I:C) LMW, GFP-dsRNA, OsHV-1 dsRNA and OsHV-1 ssRNA
dose_treatment: 19 ug poly(I:C) HMW per g oyster flesh in 20-40 uL injected into the adductor muscle vs filtered seawater; dose-response run from 1.9 ng to 19 ug per g, protection detectable from 0.019 ug per g; bath route also effective at 0.76 and 0.38 ug/mL for 2.5 h
duration: single injection
challenge: OsHV-1 uVar challenge by injection of viral suspension (titre not recoverable from the open-access text -- superscript exponent lost in conversion; consult the PDF before quoting a titre) at 1, 14, 28, 56 and 126 d post-priming
readouts: survival (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank); OsHV-1 DNA load by qPCR; poly(I:C) persistence in seawater and haemolymph by immuno-northern blot (J2 anti-dsRNA)
effect_magnitude: Survival 89-96% in poly(I:C)-primed oysters at all five challenge timepoints from 1 to 126 d post-priming; in the nucleic-acid comparison poly(I:C) HMW gave 100% and LMW 97% survival vs 20% survival (80% mortality) in filtered-seawater controls; other nucleic acids 83-90%; viral DNA below qPCR detection limit in poly(I:C) groups
replication: 3 replicate tanks per condition; 1200 spat primed per condition; 120 spat challenged per timepoint (plus 120 control-inoculum)
notes: Longest laboratory persistence window in the sub-literature. Critically, poly(I:C) itself was undetectable in haemolymph by 24 h and in seawater by 48 h, so protection at 126 d cannot be residual elicitor. Protection was virus-specific: poly(I:C)-primed oysters challenged with Vibrio crassostreae LGP32 reached only 13% survival vs 24% in controls. Results reproduced across cohorts of different genetic background

stressor: poly(I:C) HMW (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: 19 ug poly(I:C) HMW per g oyster (2016 deployment) or 10 ug per oyster (2015 deployment) by adductor-muscle injection vs filtered seawater or non-treated
duration: single injection at 126, 99, 71 or 1 d before field deployment
challenge: natural OsHV-1 disease outbreak after deployment in the Thau lagoon, Mediterranean (2015 and 2016 seasons)
readouts: survival during a natural outbreak; OsHV-1 DNA load by qPCR
effect_magnitude: 2015 deployment: 80% survival in poly(I:C)-primed vs 29% in non-treated (+51 percentage points), survival maintained 119 d after immersion; 2016 deployment: 83-92% survival across all four priming lead times, protection maintained to the end of the experiment at 156 d (>5 months); viral loads reduced but detectable in primed oysters from 14 d post-immersion
replication: 100 oysters per condition for mortality monitoring plus 72 for sampling; two independent deployments in successive years
notes: The only field/natural-outbreak validation of immune priming in a marine invertebrate, and the longest protection duration reported anywhere in this literature (156 d). Mortality in controls only began 30 d after immersion, so the field window includes both a long priming interval and a long observation period

stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: not reported (poly(I:C) exposure of mothers and of fathers separately prior to spawning; dose not stated in retrievable text)
duration: single parental exposure before spawning
challenge: OsHV-1 exposure of F1 larvae
readouts: F1 larval survival to OsHV-1; F1 larval transcriptome (RNA-seq) in unchallenged larvae
effect_magnitude: Larvae had higher survival to OsHV-1 when mothers, but not fathers, were exposed to poly(I:C) before spawning (percentages not in the retrievable text); RNA-seq gave no evidence that parental poly(I:C) exposure reconfigures antiviral gene expression in unchallenged larvae
concordance: Discordant (survival phenotype present but no corresponding transcriptomic reconfiguration in unchallenged larvae)
replication: not reported
notes: Resolves the transmission route of oyster TGIP as maternal, not paternal. A rare explicit phenotype/molecular discordance: the authors conclude maternal provisioning of antiviral compounds in eggs is more likely than transcriptional or epigenetic reprogramming

stressor: poly(I:C) HMW (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: 19 ug poly(I:C) HMW per g oyster in 40 uL injected into the adductor muscle vs filtered seawater; oysters were a biparental family (F11) 100% susceptible to POMS
duration: single injection; animals held at 15 C
challenge: OsHV-1 injection challenge at 10 d post-priming (1.32 x 10^n copies DP gene per oyster) in the short-term arm and at 126 d post-priming (1.22 x 10^n copies DP gene per uL) in the long-term arm
readouts: survival (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank); OsHV-1 DNA load by qPCR and viral transcript counts from RNA-seq; host hemocyte/whole-animal transcriptome at 1, 14, 56 and 126 d post-priming
effect_magnitude: 10 d arm: 100% survival in poly(I:C)-primed vs 5% in filtered-seawater controls at 10 d post-challenge (+95 percentage points, log-rank p<0.0001, n=60); viral DNA load 200-fold lower at 1 d post-challenge. 126 d arm: significant survival advantage retained (log-rank p<0.0001, n=45); sustained upregulation of interferon-pathway and apoptosis genes maintained over 4 months
replication: 4 replicate 5-L tanks per condition; 15 oysters per tank for survival (n=60) plus 75 per tank for sampling; long-term arm 45 oysters (15 per tank, 3 tanks); 3 pools of 15 (short arm) or 3 pools of 3 (long arm) per sampling point
notes: Mechanistic anchor for the sustained-response model: priming reverses a genetically POMS-susceptible family from susceptible to resistant. Notably the elevated immune baseline did NOT produce a strong secondary response on infection - it is a persistent alert state, not a recall response. No survival cost detected over the 4-month priming period, in contrast to the larval costs reported by Robinson & Green 2020

stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: not reported (poly(I:C) treatment of mothers; dose not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single maternal treatment before spawning
challenge: none (baseline only) - offspring traits measured without pathogen challenge; the OsHV-1 survival benefit is taken from prior work
readouts: F1 larval size; total bacterial load and Vibrio load in larvae (microbiome)
effect_magnitude: Larvae produced from poly(I:C)-treated mothers were smaller and carried higher total bacterial and Vibrio loads than control larvae (magnitudes not in the retrievable text)
replication: not reported
notes: The key trade-off paper in this sub-literature: the maternal antiviral priming benefit is paid for in larval growth rate and microbiome destabilisation. Directly opposes Cheng et al. 2024, where inactivated-Vibrio priming of oyster larvae accelerated growth and settlement

stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic)
dose_treatment: 250 ug poly I:C per oyster in 50 uL injected into the adductor muscle vs 50 uL sterile artificial seawater and vs OsHV-1-free oyster tissue homogenate; triploid spat 20-30 mm
duration: single injection; 14 d at 18 C then temperature raised to 22 C over 6 h
challenge: injection of virulent OsHV-1 (6 x 10^n genome copies per oyster) at 22 C, 21 d (3 weeks) after priming; monitored 14 d
readouts: cumulative mortality over 14 d post-challenge with PCR confirmation; OsHV-1 DNA concentration at death and in survivors; OsHV-1 prevalence in survivors
effect_magnitude: 0% mortality in the poly I:C group vs 53% in the sterile-seawater control and 55% in the tissue-homogenate control; hazard ratio 0.02 (Cox PH, tank as random effect); OsHV-1 DNA undetectable in all poly I:C survivors vs 70% prevalence in seawater-primed survivors (odds ratio 0.02)
replication: 80 oysters per treatment group; 20 oysters per tank; 4 water baths of 6 tanks; sample size powered at 80% for HR 4
notes: Only study to benchmark poly I:C directly against live and inactivated virus in one design. Authors flag that poly I:C is unlikely to be acceptable in food oysters given mammalian toxicity (mortality at 30 mg/kg in rhesus monkeys, 5 mg/kg in beagles) and that duration of protection and residue/withholding data are absent

stressor: heat-inactivated OsHV-1 (50 C for 20 min); sublethal infectious OsHV-1 administered at a non-permissive 18 C
dose_treatment: 3 x 10^n OsHV-1 genome copies per oyster in 50 uL injected into the adductor muscle, either heat-inactivated or infectious, vs 50 uL sterile artificial seawater and vs OsHV-1-free tissue homogenate
duration: single injection; 14 d at 18 C then temperature raised to 22 C
challenge: injection of virulent OsHV-1 (6 x 10^n genome copies per oyster) at 22 C, 21 d after priming; monitored 14 d
readouts: cumulative mortality over 14 d post-challenge; mortality during the 21 d priming phase; OsHV-1 DNA load and prevalence in survivors
effect_magnitude: Cumulative mortality 26.7% with heat-inactivated OsHV-1 (hazard ratio 0.41, relative percent survival 51.5%) and 12.8% with infectious OsHV-1 (HR 0.18, RPS 76.8%) vs 53% in the sterile-seawater control; 12.5% (95% CI 8.2-18.6) mortality occurred during the priming phase in the infectious group only, and none in any other group
replication: 80 oysters per treatment (160 for the infectious-OsHV-1 group to allow for priming mortality); 20 oysters per tank
notes: Establishes that viral replication is NOT required to induce protection (heat-inactivated virus worked), but that live priming is stronger than inactivated, implying an additional replication-dependent (e.g. RNAi) component on top of the PAMP effect. Inactivated virus avoids the 12.5% priming mortality and the biosecurity risk of moving infected stock

stressor: sublethal live Pinctada birnavirus (PiBV) infection at a non-permissive low water temperature
dose_treatment: PiBV 4.4 x 10^n copies per container, 1 h static immersion of approximately 370 acclimated juveniles, at low water temperature 18-20 C (non-lethal) vs uninfected controls; high-temperature 24-25 C controls used to show lethality
duration: 1 h immersion; then 28 d at 18-20 C before acclimation to 24-25 C over 7 d
challenge: re-infection with PiBV (8.7 x 10^n copies per dish, 1 h immersion) at 24-25 C, 35 d after the first infection; mortality followed 22 d; plus ex vivo PiBV challenge of mantle explants from survivors at 96 d post-infection
readouts: cumulative mortality; mantle atrophy; PiBV load in tissue and viral shedding into seawater; PiBV replication in ex vivo mantle explants; transcriptome at 28 d post-infection
effect_magnitude: 10% mortality in previously infected survivors vs approximately 50% in naive oysters challenged under identical high-temperature conditions (-40 percentage points, significant); first infection at 24-25 C in naive juveniles caused approximately 80% mortality whereas mortality at 18-20 C was <30% and not different from uninfected controls; PiBV replication significantly reduced in mantle explants from previously infected oysters
replication: 3 subgroups of 20 individuals per group in the re-infection trial; 50 oysters per 8 L aquarium in the first infection; mantle explants from individual oysters in 48-well plates
notes: Only non-herpesvirus bivalve virus system in this table and the only one showing tissue-autonomous resistance: mantle explants alone resisted PiBV. Important caveat the authors raise themselves - culture supernatants of survivor explants were PiBV-RNA-positive without inoculation, so persistent low-level infection may sustain the primed state rather than true immune memory. Interferon-like genes showed no appreciable change, so the mechanism is unresolved

stressor: live or heat-killed Vibrio splendidus
dose_treatment: not reported (live vs heat-killed V. splendidus exposure; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single priming exposure
challenge: live Vibrio splendidus challenge; plus adoptive transfer of cell-free plasma or haemocytes from primed to naive mussels
readouts: survival; total haemocyte concentration; haemocyte population profiles; phagocytic activity; lysosomal function; ROS production; adoptive-transfer protection of naive recipients
effect_magnitude: Markedly higher survival during subsequent bacterial challenge with protection lasting at least 21 days (percentages not in the retrievable text); both cell-free plasma and haemocytes from primed mussels conveyed protection to naive individuals; sustained increase in total haemocyte concentration, altered phagocytosis, enhanced lysosomal function and a biphasic ROS pattern
replication: not reported
notes: First demonstration of immune priming in the blue mussel and the first transferable (adoptive) immune memory in a bivalve - protection resides in both a humoral and a cellular compartment. Live and heat-killed bacteria triggered distinct cellular responses, implying different activation pathways for the same protective outcome

stressor: repeated sublethal Vibrio alginolyticus challenge
dose_treatment: not reported (repeated V. alginolyticus challenge; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: repeated challenges (interval not stated in the retrievable text)
challenge: live Vibrio alginolyticus challenge
readouts: mortality rate and timing; haemocyte viability; pathogen recognition, inflammatory and apoptosis responses; antioxidant enzyme responses; tissue-specific analysis of haemocytes, gill and digestive gland
effect_magnitude: Immune-primed mussels showed slower mortality and maintained higher haemocyte viability than non-primed mussels (magnitudes not in the retrievable text)
concordance: Partial (gill showed immune tolerance while digestive gland showed sustained immune and antioxidant responses - the two tissues diverged)
replication: not reported
notes: Best evidence in the bivalve literature that the primed state is tissue-specific rather than systemic and uniform: gill tolerised while digestive gland sustained both immune and antioxidant responses. A caution against whole-animal molecular readouts of priming

stressor: sublethal Vibrio anguillarum injection
dose_treatment: not reported (V. anguillarum injection vs PBS injection control; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single injection
challenge: second Vibrio anguillarum injection 7 d after the first (AA group) vs PBS-primed then challenged (SS/SA controls)
readouts: survival (log-rank); hepatopancreas bacterial load; alkaline and acid phosphatase, SOD and MDA activities; hepatopancreas transcriptome
effect_magnitude: Survival of the twice-injected AA group significantly higher than all control groups after the second injection (log-rank p<0.05); pathogen clearance from hepatopancreas significantly enhanced; AKP, ACP, SOD and MDA all significantly higher after secondary than after primary stimulation
concordance: Concordant (84 DEGs commonly upregulated after both primary and secondary stimulation, including C-type mannose receptor 2, ATG12 and TLR4)
replication: not reported
notes: First evidence of immune priming in the Manila clam; uses the same 7-day priming window that recurs across the bivalve and crustacean literature, suggesting a de facto field convention rather than an empirically optimised interval

stressor: inactivated Vibrio splendidus
dose_treatment: not reported (inactivated V. splendidus stimulation of middle-umbo larvae at 10 days post-fertilisation; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single stimulation at 10 dpf
challenge: live Vibrio splendidus challenge of late-umbo larvae (18 dpf) or pediveliger larvae (21 dpf)
readouts: larval death rate at two later stages; immune receptor and effector gene expression (CTL-3, Integrin beta-1, TLR4, IKK, IL17-5, Defh2, HSP70); SOD, CAT and lysozyme activities; agglutination and growth inhibition of V. splendidus by larval proteins; shell height and length, development rate, settlement rate
effect_magnitude: Much lower death rate in the stimulated group than controls when challenged at either 18 dpf (8 d post-priming) or 21 dpf (11 d post-priming); significantly increased shell height and length, accelerated development rate and higher settlement rate in primed larvae (magnitudes not in the retrievable text)
replication: not reported
notes: Ontogenic priming across larval stages, with two post-priming challenge timepoints (8 and 11 d). Notably priming IMPROVED growth, development and settlement rather than costing them - the direct opposite of the poly(I:C) maternal-priming cost reported by Robinson & Green 2020, suggesting the trade-off depends on elicitor and stage

stressor: low-dose formalin-inactivated Vibrio alginolyticus; compared with live Vibrio alginolyticus priming
dose_treatment: low-dose formalin-inactivated V. alginolyticus at 5 x 10^n and 5 x 10^n CFU/mL (exponents not recoverable from the indexed text); the trans-generational arm used immersion at 5 x 10^n CFU/mL; live V. alginolyticus priming tested as a comparison
duration: single priming exposure (injection or immersion)
challenge: secondary Vibrio alginolyticus infection of primed adults; challenge of F1 larvae with several different Vibrio species
readouts: adult mortality; haemocyte ROS level and necrosis; F1 larval resistance to multiple Vibrio species
effect_magnitude: Low-dose formalin-inactivated V. alginolyticus protected adults against secondary V. alginolyticus infection; priming with LIVE V. alginolyticus instead raised ROS, caused haemocyte necrosis and produced HIGHER late-stage mortality (a maladaptive outcome); trans-generational priming significantly increased larval resistance to various Vibrio species
replication: not reported
notes: Dose and elicitor form are decisive: live-pathogen priming was actively harmful while low-dose inactivated priming was protective - one of the few explicit maladaptive priming results in this literature. Offspring protection was broad-spectrum across Vibrio species rather than strain-specific, which conflicts with the specificity reported by Zuo et al. 2025 and Pope et al. 2011

stressor: live Vibrio splendidus injection of gonad-matured parents
dose_treatment: 100 uL of Vibrio splendidus suspension at 2 x 10^n CFU/mL injected into gonad-matured adults vs an equal volume of sterile seawater; maternal and paternal priming tested in separate arms
duration: single injection; artificial spawning and fertilisation performed 7 d post-priming
challenge: Vibrio splendidus exposure of embryos/larvae at 1 x 10^n CFU/mL from the blastula stage (4.5 h post-fertilisation)
readouts: egg lysozyme, SOD, NO and glucose; egg antibacterial activity; larval mortality and hatching rate; CAT, lysozyme and SOD through early ontogeny; larval transcriptome; DNMT1, DNMT3a and DNMT3b expression; E3 ligase expression
effect_magnitude: Larval mortality significantly lower and hatching rate significantly higher in both maternal (mVs-Vs) and paternal (pVs-Vs) primed groups than in naive-parent challenged controls (nSw-Vs); egg lysozyme activity 0.486 ug/mL in maternally primed vs 0.28 ug/mL in controls (p<0.05); egg SOD, NO and glucose all significantly elevated at 7 d post-priming
concordance: Partial (maternal arm showed both enzyme and gene-expression changes; paternal arm showed gene-expression changes with no detectable enzyme changes)
replication: 160 gonad-matured adults split across 2 priming groups; approximately 3,000,000 embryos per tank; 3 biological replicates each pooled from 3 parallel samples
notes: First bacteria-induced TGIP in a mollusc, and the closest any paper in this set comes to an epigenetic mechanism for transgenerational priming: all three DNMTs were significantly upregulated during early ontogeny in maternally primed offspring and rose sharply only at the D-veliger stage in paternally primed offspring. CRITICAL CAVEAT - DNA methylation itself was never measured, only DNMT transcript abundance

stressor: sublethal Vibrio splendidus vs Staphylococcus aureus pre-stimulation
dose_treatment: not reported (V. splendidus or S. aureus pre-stimulation; concentration and route not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single pre-stimulation
challenge: secondary Vibrio splendidus stimulation
readouts: haemocyte phagocytic activity against V. splendidus, S. aureus and inert fluorescent microspheres; CgbetaGBP2, CgC1qDC-8, CgRab24, CgBigdefensin1 and CgBigdefensin2 expression; NO level; lysozyme in hepatopancreas and cell-free haemolymph; haemolymph growth-inhibition assay; histone marks H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K9ac and H3K27ac
effect_magnitude: Phagocytic activity against V. splendidus (but not against S. aureus or inert microspheres) significantly higher in V. splendidus-primed than in S. aureus-primed oysters; CgbetaGBP2, CgC1qDC-8, CgRab24, CgBigdefensin1/2 and NO all significantly up; lysozyme up in hepatopancreas and cell-free haemolymph with stronger inhibition of V. splendidus growth; first stimulation with EITHER microbe significantly increased H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K9ac and H3K27ac
concordance: Partial (the functional protection was pathogen-specific whereas the global histone-mark increase was induced equally by the non-protective Gram-positive microbe)
replication: not reported
notes: Strongest evidence for pathogen specificity of the functional priming response in an oyster. But because bulk histone marks rose equally after a microbe that conferred no protection, global chromatin marks cannot be the carrier of that specificity - promoter-level resolution (as in Lian et al. 2024) is required

stressor: sublethal dose of a sympatric or an allopatric Vibrio splendidus strain
dose_treatment: sublethal dose of bacterial cells of two closely related V. splendidus strains differing in virulence, one isolated at the same location as the oysters (sympatric) and one from a different location (allopatric); concentrations not stated in the retrievable text
duration: single priming exposure
challenge: potentially lethal dose of sympatric or allopatric Vibrio splendidus, assessed both in vitro on cell-free haemolymph plasma and in vivo
readouts: in vitro bacterial growth in cell-free haemolymph plasma; in vivo bacterial loads
effect_magnitude: Priming produced inhibitory effects on subsequent bacterial growth in vitro, strongest when primed with the sympatric strain but with partial cross-protection against the allopatric strain; addition of haemolymph plasma generally promoted growth of both strains; in vivo bacterial loads INCREASED after the initial challenge, contradicting the in vitro result
concordance: Discordant (in vitro humoral priming effect was not reflected in the in vivo infection data)
replication: not reported
notes: Essential negative/discordant result for the field: an in vitro priming signal did not translate into in vivo protection. Also the only test of local adaptation in priming specificity - stronger priming against the co-occurring strain suggests a host-pathogen co-evolutionary component

stressor: inactivated Vibrio splendidus
dose_treatment: not reported (inactivated V. splendidus for primary stimulation, live V. splendidus for secondary; concentrations not stated in the retrievable text); pharmacological arms used the histone methyltransferase inhibitor 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and the histone demethylase inhibitor monomethyl fumarate (MEF)
duration: single primary stimulation
challenge: secondary Vibrio splendidus stimulation 7 d after the primary stimulation
readouts: CgTLR3, CgMyD88-2 and CgIL17-1 expression at 6 h after primary vs 6 h after secondary stimulation; H3K4me3 ChIP enrichment at the CgTLR3 promoter at 7 d post-priming; inhibitor rescue experiments
effect_magnitude: CgTLR3, CgMyD88-2 and CgIL17-1 expression at 6 h after secondary stimulation significantly higher than at 6 h after primary (p<0.05); H3K4me3 enrichment at the CgTLR3 promoter significantly increased at 7 d after primary stimulation with inactivated V. splendidus (p<0.05); MTA reduced both the mark and the secondary-response gene expression (p<0.05) while MEF increased both (p<0.05)
replication: not reported
notes: The clearest causal epigenetic evidence in any bivalve: a specific histone mark deposited at a named promoter during the 7-day priming window is both necessary (MTA) and sufficient-enhancing (MEF) for the amplified secondary response. Limitation - no survival or organismal protection endpoint; the phenotype is gene expression only

stressor: Vibrio splendidus stimulation
dose_treatment: not reported (V. splendidus stimulation; concentration not stated in the retrievable text); pharmacological/RNAi arms used the KDM5 activator DM-alpha-ketoglutarate and CgKDM5A RNAi
duration: single primary stimulation
challenge: secondary Vibrio splendidus stimulation 7 d after the primary stimulation
readouts: CgKDM5A transcript level and KDM5 enzymatic activity; global H3K4me3; H3K4me3 ChIP enrichment at CgBMP7 and CgGATA2/3 promoters at 7 d; haemocyte proliferation index at 12 h post-secondary stimulation
effect_magnitude: CgKDM5A transcripts and KDM5 activity significantly decreased after V. splendidus stimulation with a corresponding increase in H3K4me3; H3K4me3 at CgBMP7 and CgGATA2/3 promoters elevated at 7 d post-priming (p<0.05); haemocyte proliferation index significantly increased at 12 h after secondary stimulation (p<0.05); KDM5 activator DM-alphaKG raised promoter H3K4me3 at 7 d but then reduced CgBMP7/CgGATA2/3 expression and proliferation after secondary stimulation, while CgKDM5A-RNAi enriched the mark and increased proliferation
replication: not reported
notes: Links the epigenetic priming window to haematopoiesis: H3K4me3 at developmental transcription-factor promoters licenses haemocyte proliferation on re-challenge. Same 7-day window as Lian et al. 2024. No organismal protection endpoint

stressor: Vibrio splendidus stimulation
dose_treatment: not reported (V. splendidus stimulation; concentration not stated in the retrievable text); loss-of-function arms used RNAi of CgCLec-HTM/IgR, Syk and BCL10 plus the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin and the ERK inhibitor FR180204
duration: single primary stimulation
challenge: secondary Vibrio splendidus stimulation (assessed 6 h post-secondary); molecular state assessed 7 d after the first stimulation
readouts: mTOR and ERK phosphorylation; glycolysis genes CgGluT and CgGK; NAD+/NADH ratio; lactate concentration; H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 levels; haemocyte phagocytic rate; CgClathrin, CgATPeV and CgTNF expression
effect_magnitude: Silencing CgCLec-HTM/IgR-Syk-BCL10 significantly reduced mTOR and ERK phosphorylation at 6 h post-primary and reduced CgGluT/CgGK expression, NAD+/NADH ratio, lactate, H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 at 7 d post-primary, plus haemocyte phagocytic rate and CgClathrin/CgATPeV/CgTNF at both 7 d post-primary and 6 h post-secondary; rapamycin and FR180204 independently reproduced the loss of glycolytic output and of H3K4me1/H3K4me3
replication: not reported
notes: Demonstrates metabolic-epigenetic coupling in a bivalve - a lectin receptor drives glycolysis via mTOR/ERK, and glycolytic output in turn sets H3K4 methylation levels - closely paralleling mammalian trained immunity and the shrimp KAT8/acetyl-CoA axis of Lv et al. 2025. Loss-of-function only; no survival endpoint

stressor: poly(I:C); filtered-seawater injection used as a sterile-injury control elicitor
dose_treatment: not reported (poly I:C stimulation of mussels/haemocytes; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single stimulation
challenge: waterborne viral haemorrhagic septicaemia virus (VHSV) exposure
readouts: haemocyte transcriptome including lncRNAs (RNA-seq); rate of viral clearance by haemocytes; IL-17, IRF1 and viperin expression
effect_magnitude: Both poly I:C and a sterile filtered-seawater injection accelerated VHSV clearance by haemocytes and altered expression of several immune genes including IL-17, IRF1 and viperin; the poly I:C transcriptomic response was dominated by apoptosis and an IRF/STING-IFI44/IRGC1 axis with lncRNA modulation
concordance: Partial (a sterile injury control reproduced part of the protective effect, so the response is not poly(I:C)-specific)
replication: not reported
notes: Important methodological control that most of this literature omits: sterile seawater injection ALONE accelerated viral clearance, meaning wounding/damage signals can mimic PAMP priming. Ecological relevance is limited because mussels are not naturally susceptible to VHSV

stressor: ultraviolet-inactivated white spot syndrome virus (UV-WSSV, 30 min UV)
dose_treatment: 50 uL UV-inactivated WSSV containing approximately 1.0 x 10^n genome copies injected intramuscularly at the third abdominal segment vs 50 uL PBS; shrimp approximately 10 g
duration: single injection; 20-22 C recirculating seawater, salinity 35 ppt
challenge: live WSSV (1.0 x 10^n copies in 50 uL PBS) injected 5 d after the priming injection
readouts: survival (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank); WSSV copy number in hemocytes and intestine; VP28 protein; global H3K27ac, H4K16ac and H3K9ac; ChIP-qPCR of H3K27ac at the Dorsal promoter and at Hk2, Pk and Ldh promoters; Vago5 and AMP expression; glycolysis and TCA metabolites; acetyl-CoA; KAT8 RNAi and MG149 inhibitor rescue
effect_magnitude: Survival of UV-WSSV-trained shrimp significantly higher than PBS-trained controls after WSSV infection (Kaplan-Meier log-rank; percentages presented in figures only); KAT8 RNAi or the KAT8 inhibitor MG149 abolished the UV-WSSV-induced H3K27ac increase, raised WSSV replication and VP28 protein, and markedly reduced survival; H3K9ac and H4K16ac were NOT increased in the trained model
replication: 30 shrimp per group with 3 replicates for survival curves; 3 independent biological replicates of 3 shrimp per group for in vivo molecular assays
notes: Mechanistically the strongest epigenetic trained-immunity paper in any marine invertebrate: enhanced glycolysis and TCA flux raise acetyl-CoA, which fuels KAT8 to deposit H3K27ac at the NF-kB-like Dorsal promoter, driving Vago5 and AMP output, with a feed-forward loop back onto glycolytic gene promoters. The authors' own literature synthesis gives the field's duration range - formalin-inactivated WSSV protection is lost by 30 d; low-dose live WSSV protection is significant between 3 weeks and 2 months but gone by 3 months; decapod vaccine protection generally lasts 7-30 d

stressor: formalin-inactivated Vibrio parahaemolyticus (AHPND strain)
dose_treatment: three doses of formalin-inactivated V. parahaemolyticus tested; medium dose 7.5 x 10^n CFU/mL and high dose 7.5 x 10^n CFU/mL (exponents not recoverable from the indexed text) vs unprimed control
duration: single priming exposure
challenge: none (baseline only) - chromatin and extracellular-vesicle profiling of the primed state without a pathogen challenge
readouts: H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 in hemocytes by semi-quantitative immunofluorescence at days 1, 2, 4 and 7 post-priming; hemolymph extracellular vesicle size distribution and particle concentration by nano-flow cytometry at day 7
effect_magnitude: No significant difference in H3K4me3 or H3K27me3 among groups at day 1; at day 2 a significant increase in H3K4me3 only in the medium-dose group; by day 4 both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 significantly elevated in the high-dose group vs control and lower doses; by day 7 histone modification levels across all groups had largely returned to baseline; EV size distributions stable but particle concentrations altered in the high-dose group at day 7
replication: not reported (authors describe limited sample availability and single-method EV characterisation)
notes: The most explicit epigenetic DECAY curve in this entire sub-literature and the only dose x time chromatin design: bulk histone marks in shrimp hemocytes are transient (peak 2-4 d, back to baseline by 7 d) and dose-specific. This sits directly at odds with promoter-level H3K4me3 still elevated at 7 d in oysters and with 5-month functional protection in oysters, implying bulk histone marks are not the memory substrate

stressor: Aeromonas hydrophila stimulation (inactivated primary, then secondary challenge)
dose_treatment: not reported (A. hydrophila stimulation; concentration not stated in the retrievable text); loss-of-function arm used EsKDM4 RNAi
duration: single primary stimulation
challenge: secondary Aeromonas hydrophila stimulation; molecular state assessed 7 d after the first stimulation
readouts: hemocyte glucose, lactate and NAD+/NADH; EsPFK, EsPK, EsHK-2 and EsG-6-PD expression; global H3K9me3 and ChIP enrichment at EsPFK and EsG-6-PD promoters; EsKDM4 nuclear translocation and enzymatic activity
effect_magnitude: Hemocyte glucose significantly down and EsPFK/EsPK/EsHK-2/EsG-6-PD, lactate and NAD+/NADH significantly up after secondary A. hydrophila stimulation; H3K9me3 and its enrichment at the EsPFK and EsG-6-PD promoters significantly DECREASED at 7 d after stimulation; EsKDM4 RNAi restored H3K9me3 and its promoter enrichment and lowered glycolytic transcripts, lactate and NAD+/NADH after secondary stimulation
replication: not reported
notes: Sign-reversed relative to the H3K4me3/H3K27ac papers: here it is REMOVAL of a repressive mark (H3K9me3, via the demethylase KDM4) at glycolytic gene promoters that encodes the primed metabolic state. Same 7-day window. Species caveat - Eriocheir sinensis is a catadromous, estuarine-breeding crab usually cultured in fresh water, so it sits at the edge of the marine/estuarine inclusion criterion; flagged rather than excluded

stressor: heat-killed Vibrio parahaemolyticus (autoclaved 30 min at 60 C)
dose_treatment: heat-killed V. parahaemolyticus at an effective 10^n CFU per g crab in 100 uL by injection vs 100 uL sterile physiological (0.9%) saline; suspension adjusted to 3.1 x 10^n CFU/mL before inactivation
duration: single injection; immune priming phase of 168 h
challenge: injection of live Vibrio parahaemolyticus at 5.0 x 10^n CFU per g crab (a lethal dose determined in pre-experiments) 168 h (7 d) after priming
readouts: survival (log-rank); TLR signalling pathway gene expression (TLR, Spaetzle, MyD88, Pelle, Cactus, Dorsal, Dscam) and antimicrobial peptide genes (Hyastatin, Arasin, Crustin, ALF3-ALF6) in hemocytes and hepatopancreas at 6, 9 and 72 h
effect_magnitude: Survival of the heat-killed-primed then live-challenged group (HkVp+Vp) significantly higher than all other groups (log-rank p<0.05), diverging from 9 h post-challenge and widening with time; no mortality difference between primed and saline groups during the priming phase itself
replication: 250 crabs per priming group; 6 crabs per group per sampling timepoint (36 crabs sampled per group during the priming phase)
notes: Cleanly separates early-acting effectors in hemocytes (Dscam, Hyastatin, Cactus, Arasin, ALF3-ALF6) from late-acting ones (Crustin, Dorsal, Pelle, MyD88), with TLR and Spaetzle elevated throughout - a two-phase molecular architecture to the 7-day primed state. Estuarine/mangrove species, mariculture-relevant

stressor: heat-killed (HVa) or formalin-inactivated (FVa) Vibrio alginolyticus
dose_treatment: not reported (injection of heat-killed or formalin-inactivated V. alginolyticus vs saline; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single primary exposure
challenge: secondary exposure to live Vibrio alginolyticus 7 d after primary exposure; phagocytic activity and bacterial clearance also examined in 7- to 35-day-primed shrimp
readouts: mortality; haemocyte count and immune parameters; haematopoietic tissue proliferation and mitotic index; phagocytic activity; bacterial clearance efficiency
effect_magnitude: 7-day FVa-primed shrimp showed clear enhancement of immunity on secondary exposure to live V. alginolyticus with higher haematopoietic tissue proliferation and mitotic index, whereas 7-day HVa-primed shrimp showed only minor enhancement; both HVa- and FVa-primed shrimp maintained elevated phagocytic activity and bacterial clearance beyond 28 days (assessed across a 7-35 day series); HVa raised immune parameters on day 1 and FVa on day 5
replication: not reported
notes: One of very few studies to follow a priming effect out to 35 d with intermediate timepoints - phagocytosis and clearance stayed elevated past 28 d. Inactivation method changes the kinetics: formalin-inactivated behaved as a vaccine (delayed, durable, recall-competent) while heat-killed behaved as a fast, short-lived non-specific inducer/adjuvant

stressor: formalin-inactivated Vibrio harveyi; Bacillus subtilis tested as a non-pathogen elicitor
dose_treatment: not reported (formalin-inactivated V. harveyi or sterile saline injected into the haemocoel; dose not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: single injection
challenge: ex vivo incubation of haemocytes collected 7 d after injection with a 1:1 mix of Vibrio harveyi and Bacillus subtilis
readouts: haemocyte phagocytosis (percentage of phagocytic cells); humoral antibacterial activity of whole haemolymph
effect_magnitude: Haemocytes from V. harveyi-primed shrimp showed significantly elevated phagocytosis of V. harveyi but NOT of B. subtilis, driven by an increase in the percentage of phagocytic cells; shrimp injected with B. subtilis showed no increase in phagocytic activity at all; humoral antibacterial activity against V. harveyi was present but identical between primed and control shrimp
replication: not reported
notes: Localises priming specificity to the cellular (phagocytic) arm and explicitly rules out the humoral antibacterial arm. Also shows priming is not universal across microbes - B. subtilis, not a natural shrimp pathogen, failed to prime, mirroring the elicitor-specificity results of Green 2013 (bacteria do not prime against virus) and Zuo 2025

stressor: sublethal live Vibrio campbellii pre-challenge injection, with hypercapnic hypoxia as an environmental modifier
dose_treatment: pre-challenge injection of 1 x 10^5 Vibrio campbellii per g crab vs an equivalent 1 uL per g of HEPES-buffered saline, in either normoxic seawater (PO2 20.7 kPa, CO2 <0.06 kPa, pH 7.8-8.0) or hypercapnic hypoxic seawater (PO2 4 kPa, CO2 1.8 kPa, pH 6.9-7.2)
duration: single injection; water treatment maintained throughout
challenge: second injection of live Vibrio campbellii at 1 x 10^5 per g crab, delivered either 2 h or 24 h after the pre-challenge dose
readouts: clearance of culturable bacteria from haemolymph by selective plating; clearance of intact bacteria by real-time PCR; bacteriostasis; cell-free haemolymph antibacterial activity
effect_magnitude: Crabs challenged 2 h after the pre-challenge dose cleared culturable V. campbellii from haemolymph significantly faster than saline-pre-challenged crabs, with a concurrent increase in cell-free haemolymph antibacterial activity; the enhancement DISAPPEARED entirely when the interval was extended to 24 h, and was also abolished when crabs were held in hypercapnic hypoxic seawater; clearance of intact bacteria was unaffected in all treatments
replication: not reported
notes: The shortest-lived priming effect in this table and the only study with an explicit decay bracket (present at 2 h, gone by 24 h) plus an environmental modifier: low dissolved oxygen and elevated CO2 abolish the primed state. Directly relevant to whether priming survives realistic estuarine hypoxia/acidification. Also a useful null - prior bacterial exposure did NOT increase susceptibility

stressor: heat-killed Vibrio parahaemolyticus cells or heat-killed Bacillus subtilis cells
dose_treatment: not reported (exposure of developing embryos to heat-killed Vibrio or Bacillus cells; concentration not stated in the retrievable text)
duration: exposure during embryonic development
challenge: live Vibrio parahaemolyticus challenge of nauplii
readouts: hatching percentage; larval development; immune-related gene expression; nauplius resistance to bacterial infection
effect_magnitude: Percentage hatching and resistance to bacterial infection both increased in embryos treated with heat-killed Vibrio or Bacillus cells (magnitudes not in the retrievable text); Vibrio induced a strong effector immune response whereas Bacillus elicited a protective immune profile - different gene-expression patterns for a comparable protective outcome
concordance: Partial (two elicitors produced different transcriptional profiles but similar protection)
replication: not reported
notes: Rare embryo-stage priming and the earliest life stage primed in this whole set; embryo immersion is one of the few practically scalable delivery routes for shrimp hatcheries. Priming improved hatching as well as resistance, i.e. no detected cost at this stage

stressor: formalin-killed Vibrio parahaemolyticus (FKC-Vp strains TUMSAT_N3, TUMSAT_FP11, TUMSAT_D6) delivered by bath immersion
dose_treatment: bath immersion in 1% or 2% formalin-killed V. parahaemolyticus for 1 h or 2 h; optimum was 1% FKC-VpFP11 for 1 h, after which shrimp were transferred to clean tanks
duration: 1 h immersion
challenge: live Vibrio parahaemolyticus (AHPND) challenge 7 d post-vaccination
readouts: survival; hepatopancreas histopathology; hepatopancreas and stomach transcriptome at 24 h post-vaccination; qPCR of 12 immune DEGs at 24 h and 7 d post-vaccination and 24 h post-challenge
effect_magnitude: 80% survival in vaccinated shrimp vs a lower rate in unvaccinated controls (control value not stated in the retrievable text); no histopathological damage in the hepatopancreas; antimicrobial effectors GILT and hemocyanin C-chain peaked at 24 h post-vaccination while recognition factors (C-type lectin, perlucin) and putative epigenetic regulators (zinc finger, E3 ubiquitin ligase, late histone H1) remained sustained or upregulated through 7 d post-vaccination; all 12 DEGs upregulated at 24 h post-challenge with hemocyanin C-chain significantly elevated; significant time x treatment interaction for GILT
replication: not reported
notes: The only optimised immersion/bath delivery protocol in this set - the practically deployable route, since injection is unusable at commercial scale (a limitation de Kantzow et al. 2023 flag explicitly for oysters). Distinguishes a 24 h acute-phase response from a distinct 'primed state' at 7 d. Chromatin-associated transcripts (late histone H1) were sustained but no chromatin assay was performed

stressor: diel-cycling hypoxia
dose_treatment: 0.5 mg/L dissolved oxygen (8% saturation) at trough vs 100% saturation normoxic control
duration: Phase 1: 18 d containing 13 d of diel cycling (3 h drawdown, 4 h plateau at 0.5 mg/L, 3 h ramp up, 14 h control), 5 d/week; Phase 2: 18 d containing 14 d cycling
challenge: second 18 d diel-cycling hypoxia exposure applied 60 d after the first (fully crossed CC/CH/HC/HH design)
readouts: gene-body DNA methylation; differentially methylated gene counts (companion paper measured tissue and shell growth)
effect_magnitude: 196 DMGs between CH and HC; only 12 DMGs CC vs HC; 1 DMG (MDE1) CC vs HH; 0 DMGs HH vs CH; first exposure PERMANOVA R2=0.068 p=0.017 and second R2=0.076 p=0.004 across all genes; DMG-only ordination explained ~60% of variation; 0.25-1.00% of CpGs methylated
concordance: Discordant (methylome differences driven mainly by the FIRST exposure whereas the companion phenotype paper found growth driven mainly by the SECOND exposure)
replication: 12 tanks (6 per treatment) in Phase 1 with 150 oysters per container; 48 oysters per tank in Phase 2; n=5 individuals per treatment combination for methylRAD
notes: Molecular carryover effect explicitly decoupled from gross phenotype. Recent exposure overrode earlier exposure (HH vs CH = 0 DMGs). Whole-body tissue may mask tissue-specific signal; methylRAD gives low coverage; no paired gene expression. Uses the ambient-temperature subset of the Donelan et al. 2021 animals.

stressor: diel-cycling hypoxia plus warming (factorial)
dose_treatment: 0.5 mg/L dissolved oxygen trough vs 100% saturation control; elevated vs ambient temperature (temperature set points not stated in abstract)
duration: 18 d per phase containing 13-14 d of diel cycling (from companion paper)
challenge: re-exposure to the same diel-cycling hypoxia and warming treatments 8 weeks later
readouts: tissue:shell growth ratio; tissue growth; shell growth
effect_magnitude: strong interactive effect of early-life hypoxia x warming on tissue:shell growth that manifested ONLY on re-exposure two months later; numeric effect sizes not given in abstract
replication: multi-phase laboratory experiment; 150 oysters per perforated container, 12 tanks (6 per DO treatment)
notes: Carryover effects were context-dependent: invisible in benign conditions and only expressed when the stressor returned. Energy reallocation between tissue and shell is the flagged fitness concern.

stressor: 18-compound pesticide and metal mixture
dose_treatment: nominal sum concentration 2.85 ug/L (measured sum 3.74 +/- 0.013 ug/L) vs clean filtered seawater
duration: 48 h (0-48 h post fertilisation)
challenge: none (baseline only); later-life traits and field deployment of 1-year-old spat
readouts: embryo-larval abnormality at 24 hpf; larval swimming behaviour; length and weight; epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; field survival
effect_magnitude: no significant difference in 24 hpf abnormality; swimming behaviour disturbed; exposed individuals longer and heavier at specific timepoints; LOWER epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; HIGHER field survival rate
concordance: Partial (significant global demethylation trend in exposed larvae alongside differential expression of Hox orthologues and cell-cycle regulators in gastrula embryos; no direct methylation-expression coupling shown)
replication: not reported
notes: A 48 h embryonic window produced multi-scale latent effects detectable up to field deployment ~1 year later. Direction is genuinely mixed: impaired metamorphosis but improved field survival. Companion reproductive-endpoint paper (10.1016/j.scitotenv.2024.173569) reports F0 glycogen increase and higher 48 hpf reproductive success, plus F1 feminisation and accelerated gametogenesis.

stressor: 18-compound pesticide mixture
dose_treatment: nominal sum concentration 2.85 ug/L vs clean seawater
duration: 48 h (0-48 h post fertilisation) in each of two generations
challenge: direct F1 embryo-larval re-exposure to the same mixture in a 2x2 crossed design (F0 exposed/control x F1 exposed/control)
readouts: epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; field survival rate; growth
effect_magnitude: individuals descending from exposed parents had LOWER epinephrine-induced metamorphosis and LOWER field survival; the multigenerational (parental) effect had a greater influence on phenotype than direct exposure itself; negative interaction pattern for field survival (higher mortality when early exposure was combined with exposed parents)
concordance: Partial (RNA-seq and Methyl-seq in gastrula embryos and metamorphosis-competent pediveliger larvae showed clear F0-treatment-dependent discrimination; F1:F0 treatment interaction patterns for shell-secretion and immunity genes e.g. Calm and Myd88)
replication: not reported
notes: MALADAPTIVE: parental conditioning made offspring WORSE, and the ancestral effect exceeded the effect of the animals' own exposure. Strongest pollutant multigenerational dataset in this table.

stressor: marine-heatwave temperature applied during gametogenesis
dose_treatment: 18.3 C (marine heatwave) vs 13.1 C (non-marine-heatwave control)
duration: 4 months (October 2020 to January 2021), timed to coincide with the local gametogenesis window
challenge: acute thermal tolerance trial on hatched blastula embryos across 7 temperatures (17.5, 20.5, 24.7, 26.4, 28.0, 29.8, 31.1 C); offspring also reared at 18 or 13 C
readouts: embryo LT50; embryo and larval body size (2D area) at early gastrula and prism stages; egg size; egg protein and lipid content; adult survival and spawning success
effect_magnitude: embryos from marine-heatwave-acclimated females had significantly higher LT50 than progeny of 13 C females; larger early gastrula and prism body size; eggs had higher protein concentration (egg size and lipid unchanged); COUNTERVAILING COST: marine-heatwave-acclimated adults had LOWER spawning success
replication: 3 replicate 37 L tanks per temperature condition, 10 adult urchins per tank (N=60 total)
notes: Adult-level trade-off: better offspring thermal tolerance but reduced adult spawning success. Offspring challenged immediately at spawning, so persistence window is zero; no test of how long the acquired tolerance lasts. No molecular data collected.

stressor: natural in-kelp vs outside-kelp variability in temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen during gametogenesis
dose_treatment: inside kelp forest (slightly elevated pH and temperature, more predictable low-frequency variability) vs outside kelp forest, Santa Barbara Channel
duration: 6 months of in situ conditioning spanning the gametogenesis period
challenge: larvae reared at 1053 vs 435 uatm pCO2 at 15 C, then acute thermal stress (LT50)
readouts: larval LT50; larval physiological response to maternal and developmental environment
effect_magnitude: within each larval pCO2 treatment, progeny from OUTSIDE-kelp-conditioned mothers had a 0.4 C higher LT50; larvae raised at high pCO2 (1053 uatm) were more susceptible to acute thermal stress regardless of maternal origin
replication: not reported
notes: Natural conditioning contrast (field-conditioned mothers, not lab-dosed). Note the counterintuitive direction: mothers from the LESS buffered, less predictable outside-kelp environment produced the MORE thermally tolerant larvae, i.e. exposure to the more benign in-kelp refuge did not prime offspring.

stressor: ocean acidification and/or ocean warming
dose_treatment: OA pH 7.77; OW +2 C (29 C); OAW +2 C and pH 7.77; vs ambient control
duration: ~6 months, from the early juvenile stage through gonadogenesis and germline differentiation to the mature adult
challenge: embryos and larvae of acclimated parents reared in all four treatments to the 2-day pluteus stage
readouts: larval tolerance of acidification and of 29 C; larval arm length; egg size
effect_magnitude: larvae from OA and OAW parents were resilient to acidification and larvae from OW and OAW parents more tolerant of 29 C; BUT parental acclimation reduced larval arm lengths by as much as 21.4% and eggs were up to 21.8% smaller in females raised at 29 C
replication: not reported
notes: Textbook TGP trade-off: stress tolerance gained at the direct cost of offspring size and maternal provisioning. First transgenerational climate-change study on a marine macroinvertebrate in which the F0 was acclimated across its whole reproductive life.

stressor: ocean warming plus acidification (mid-century and end-century scenarios)
dose_treatment: two near-future scenarios (projected mid- and end-21st-century elevated temperature plus elevated pCO2) vs present-day ambient; exact set points not stated in abstract
duration: 18 months of F0 acclimatization before spawning; F1 then held 25 months in the same conditions
challenge: F1 reared 25 months under the same conditions; a natural selective pathogenic mortality event occurred at 10 months of F1 age
readouts: test size; righting response time; respiration rate; survival through the pathogen event; capacity to spawn
effect_magnitude: Ambient-Ambient group was 21% larger and 31% faster in righting than all other groups; respiration depressed by 59% and righting slowed by 28% when parents came from near-future conditions; after the pathogen event size and respiration differences disappeared but a 29% righting deficit remained; spawning capacity 50% (ambient parents) vs 21% (other groups)
replication: not reported
notes: MALADAPTIVE: significant NEGATIVE parental carryover effects, not acclimation. Physiological differences were erased by a selective mortality sweep while behavioural deficits persisted, i.e. decay was trait-specific. Assessments at 9, 10 and ~25 months.

stressor: ocean warming plus acidification
dose_treatment: +2 C above ambient temperature and 940 ppm pCO2 vs present-day ambient
duration: more than 6 years total; F0 wild adults plus F1 and F2 larvae and adults continuously exposed
challenge: F2 survivorship and size tracked to 720 d post-settlement; F3 larvae reared under climate-change or control conditions
readouts: F2 survivorship (>50% in all treatments) and test size; adult spawning performance; F3 larval arm and body length; F3 settlement success
effect_magnitude: no size difference among treatment groups up to 720 d post-settlement; significant NEGATIVE relationship between number of generations exposed to future ocean conditions and spawning performance; larvae could only be raised from control or 0.5-generation-exposed adults; larvae from both parental groups only reached settlement when raised under control conditions; reduced arm length under climate-change conditions plus smaller arm and body lengths from climate-change parents
replication: not reported
notes: MALADAPTIVE and CUMULATIVE: negative parental effects did not diminish across generations and for some traits INCREASED. Authors state explicitly that no evidence of transgenerational acclimation was detected. The most direct multi-generation refutation of assisted-conditioning optimism in an echinoderm. | PERSISTENCE SEMANTICS: this value is an exposure / tracking window under continuous or repeated conditioning, NOT days elapsed after conditioning ended. Do not rank it against clean-recovery-gap rows such as Drury_2022 or Lafont_2017.

stressor: reduced pH (elevated pCO2)
dose_treatment: pH 7.7 and pH 7.4 vs control pH 8.0
duration: 2 months of parental exposure during gametogenesis
challenge: sperm activated at pH 8.0, 7.7 or 7.4; larvae from each parental group reared at pH 8.0 or 7.7 for 20 days
readouts: sperm motility, velocity, ATP content, ATP consumption, respiration rate; larval mortality; larval somatic growth
effect_magnitude: POSITIVE carryover on sperm: velocity decreased more slowly and ATP content was higher in sperm developed under acidified conditions (longer sperm longevity); sperm motility and respiration unaffected. NEGATIVE carryover on larvae: reduced survival of larvae from pH 7.4 parents, with additive negative effects of parental plus larval low pH; larvae from low-pH parents showed NO increased capacity to cope with OA and all groups showed reduced somatic growth at low rearing pH
replication: not reported
notes: Stage-dependent REVERSAL: the same parental conditioning benefited the gamete stage and harmed the larval stage. Direct counterexample to positive-TGP expectations in echinoids.

stressor: reduced pH (acidified seawater)
dose_treatment: acidified seawater vs control seawater (pH and pCO2 set points not reported in abstract)
duration: two-generation rearing experiment (exposure length not reported in abstract)
challenge: larvae exposed to acidified seawater of the same pH as the parental treatment
readouts: larval survival; larval body size; larval morphology
effect_magnitude: larvae derived from parents acclimated to acidified seawater tended to have higher survival and showed less reduction in body size when exposed to the same pH, indicating a positive carry-over effect; no quantitative statistics in the abstract
concordance: Partial (expression patterns of larvae from acclimated parents were substantially different from those of larvae from non-acclimated and control parents, but no quantitative overlap reported)
replication: not reported
notes: Closed access; dose, exposure duration and replication were NOT extractable, which is a notable reporting gap for one of the few clearly POSITIVE echinoderm OA carryover results. Species is a commercial edible urchin in northern Japan.

stressor: reduced pH (elevated pCO2)
dose_treatment: pH 7.72 / 1013 +/- 12 uatm pCO2 vs pH 8.06 / 412 +/- 6 uatm pCO2
duration: 2 months of adult conditioning at treatment pCO2 (preceded by 2 months acclimation to aquarium seawater; 4 months total in Menai Straits water before spawning)
challenge: larvae spawned and reared at ~1000 uatm; separate acute heat shock of 25 C for 1 h applied to adults and to 2 and 4 dpf larvae
readouts: larval transcriptome at 2, 3 and 4 dpf; HSP70 and HSP90 transcript induction by qPCR; larval morphometrics and abnormality rate
effect_magnitude: larvae from low-pH-acclimated adults up-regulated antioxidants (glutathione-S-transferase family), CypP450 detoxification genes and small HSPs, i.e. maternal transcript pre-loading; larvae reared in low pH had 25-40% abnormalities and significantly smaller body length:width ratio (F=8.035, p=0.005); early larvae could not mount a full heat shock response (2 HSP transcripts up at 2 dpf, 5 at 4 dpf vs 8 in adults)
concordance: Partial (transcriptional frontloading of antioxidants is concordant with previously reported improved larval performance under low pH, but larval morphology remained impaired)
replication: 5 females and 2 males successfully spawned per treatment with gametes pooled; 3 replicate larval cultures per treatment
notes: Mechanistic case for maternal pre-loading of protective transcripts. Caveat stated by the authors: the 2-month conditioning did NOT cover the whole reproductive cycle. Larval morphological impairment persisted despite the molecular priming.

stressor: elevated temperature
dose_treatment: ~+3 C above ambient (21 C vs 18 C ambient/laboratory control)
duration: ~15 months of dam and sire exposure
challenge: offspring reared at elevated (21 C) or ambient (18 C) temperature
readouts: fertilization success; hatchability; larval survival; larval size traits; abnormality; metamorphosis
effect_magnitude: no transgenerational effect on fertilization or metamorphosis; NEGATIVE transgenerational effects on hatchability and on most larval size traits; S. intermedius probably cannot achieve transgenerational acclimation to long-term elevated temperature for survival when offspring are also at elevated temperature; dam and sire effects were highly trait- and stage-dependent
concordance: Discordant (companion transcriptome study on the same F0/F1 animals, Shi et al. 2020, 10.1038/s41598-020-64872-x, found 1891 DEGs from parental thermal history at ambient and 2203 at high developmental temperature, with 904 shared DEGs changing in the same direction and FEWER DEGs between developmental temperatures in embryos of warm parents - a molecular frontloading signature that maps onto WORSE performance)
replication: breeding design with multiple dams and sires (n per cross not stated in abstract); companion transcriptome used 3 biological replicates per group (12 mRNA libraries)
notes: MALADAPTIVE: explicit failure of transgenerational acclimation despite 15 months of parental conditioning. Valuable because it pairs a negative phenotype with a strong molecular response (see concordance field).

stressor: maternal temperature shift timed to early vs late oogenesis
dose_treatment: mothers reared at 24 C then shifted to 18 C or to 30 C
duration: thermal cue applied at either an early or a late stage of oogenesis (exact durations not stated in abstract)
challenge: adult offspring acclimated to 18 or 30 C, then upper and lower thermal tolerance limits measured (onset of spasms, lethal temperature)
readouts: offspring upper and lower thermal tolerance limits measured at the adult stage
effect_magnitude: EARLY-oogenesis cue: mothers produced offspring with greater cold AND heat tolerance whenever mother-offspring temperatures did NOT match (anticipatory maternal effect); LATE-oogenesis cue: more tolerant offspring when temperatures PERSISTED across generations; the maternal effect disappears as traits approach the upper sublethal and lethal limits
replication: reproductive pairs isolated in 20 ml glass bowls (n per treatment not stated in abstract)
notes: The single most important design lesson in this table: the DIRECTION of transgenerational plasticity reverses depending on the timing of the maternal cue within oogenesis. Also notable that the maternal effect persisted into the ADULT offspring stage, against the usual expectation that maternal effects fade early.

stressor: ocean warming, ocean acidification, and their combination
dose_treatment: OW +3 C; OA pH -0.5 units; OWA +3 C and pH -0.5; vs control conditions
duration: full parental generation exposure across the life cycle
challenge: F1 exposed to the same OW, OA or OWA conditions (trans-generational) vs F1 exposed with control parents (within-generational)
readouts: fecundity; egg volume; juvenile growth rate; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
effect_magnitude: trans-generational OW exposure FULLY alleviated the within-generation reduction in fecundity and egg volume, accompanied by increased metabolic activity; within-generation OA reduced juvenile growth rates and egg volume, and trans-generational OA exposure alleviated the growth deficit but could NOT restore egg volume (mean egg volume still ~10% below control); OWA had no negative impacts either within- or trans-generationally
replication: n=12 replicate breeding pairs per treatment for fecundity
notes: Explicitly framed as a test of human-assisted trans-generational conditioning as a conservation/restoration and aquaculture tool. Authors' conclusion is the useful caution: trans-generational exposure does not always improve traits and may not be a universally useful tool.

stressor: elevated temperature, and elevated temperature combined with elevated salinity
dose_treatment: 30 C (+3 C above the 27 C control) and 39 ppt elevated salinity vs control temperature and salinity; salinity alone was not tested
duration: entire lifespan, both within-generation and trans-generation; transplants performed at either the egg-mass or the juvenile stage
challenge: F1 exposed to the same elevated-temperature or temperature+salinity conditions; reciprocal transplants at egg-mass vs juvenile stage
readouts: juvenile growth rate; maximum body size; longevity; lifespan fecundity; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
effect_magnitude: trans-generation exposure restored 20% (elevated temperature) and 21% (temperature plus salinity) of lifespan fecundity; under temperature+salinity, worms transplanted at the egg-mass stage grew slower with lower energy-metabolism enzyme activity but reached a larger maximum body size and lived longer than those transplanted as juveniles; trans-generation elevated temperature created a trade-off in which slower-growing juveniles had greater lifespan fecundity
replication: not reported
notes: One of very few marine-invertebrate designs that includes SALINITY conditioning. Only ~20% of the fecundity deficit was recovered, i.e. partial rescue at best. The TIMING of the transplant itself generated life-history trade-offs, so developmental window matters as much as dose.

stressor: reduced salinity
dose_treatment: 26 ppt (low) vs 35 ppt (normal) seawater
duration: 2 weeks of adult exposure before reproduction; parents could be switched back and forth between salinities
challenge: in vitro fertilization and larval rearing in matched vs mismatched salinity; larvae switched from natal to non-natal salinity immediately after fertilization or 2 or 4 days after fertilization, with survival scored 2 days after each switch
readouts: sperm head area and tail length; egg morphology; fertilization success; larval survival
effect_magnitude: both mothers and fathers adaptively adjusted gamete phenotype to maximise performance in the parental salinity regime; sperm from low-salinity fathers were much smaller while egg morphology did not change; STRONG performance trade-offs whenever gametes experienced a salinity that did not match the parents; larvae switched on the day of fertilization had the LOWEST survival and later switches progressively higher survival; the parental-environment effect persisted for the whole larval phase
replication: 4 tubs per salinity treatment; sperm from 3 males and eggs from 3 females pooled per assay
notes: Best available demonstration that conditioning MANUFACTURES phenotype-environment mismatch: conditioned larvae are effectively unable to disperse to non-natal salinities, so gamete plasticity becomes a source of reduced connectivity. Parents could reverse the gamete phenotype based on their most recent experience, i.e. the memory is short and rewritable.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: maternal colonies 300 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control; larvae subsequently 50 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control
duration: 6 h maternal exposure after larval release, then colonies returned to their field site to brood the test larvae
challenge: larval copper exposure at 50 ug/L, then settlement and growth to maturity in the field with survival and growth tracked weekly for 6 weeks
readouts: larval size at emergence; post-metamorphic survival; adult colony growth in the field
effect_magnitude: in the population with NO historical copper exposure (Boat Ramp), maternal copper exposure had a strong NEGATIVE carryover effect on adult offspring growth and survival, worst when larvae were themselves also exposed; in the population WITH a copper history (Marina) there was little to no maternal or offspring treatment effect on adult growth and survival, and those parents produced larger larvae on average and increased larval size in response to copper; significant effect of population on F1 growth after 6 weeks in the field (LMM p<0.05)
replication: split-brood design across 2 populations with copper and control maternal treatments crossed with copper and control larval treatments (n per cell not extracted)
notes: MALADAPTIVE in naive populations: the direction of transgenerational plasticity is itself a locally adapted trait. Persistence figure is the 6-week post-settlement field tracking window; the interval between the end of maternal exposure and larval release (field brooding) was not resolved to days.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: copper exposure of maternal colonies vs toxicant-naive control (concentration not stated in abstract; cited by Neylan et al. 2022 as the basis for their 300 ug/L, 6 h protocol)
duration: laboratory copper exposure of maternal colonies followed by 1 week in the field to brood offspring
challenge: offspring copper resistance assay, then 6 weeks in the field under low vs high intraspecific competition
readouts: larval size; larval dispersal duration; larval copper resistance; post-metamorphic survival and performance
effect_magnitude: offspring of toxicant-exposed mothers were LARGER, more dispersive and more copper-resistant than offspring of naive mothers; BUT maternal exposure history had pervasive NEGATIVE effects on post-metamorphic performance, particularly survival, after 6 weeks in the field, especially under high intraspecific competition
replication: not reported
notes: The canonical stage-reversal / maladaptive result: conditioning improves performance in one life-history stage and reduces it in the next. Author's interpretation is that this cost is precisely why pollution resistance is INDUCED rather than constitutively expressed. Persistence figure combines the ~1 week brooding period and the 6-week field assessment.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: 100 ug/L Cu (as CuCl2.2H2O, Cu2+) vs artificial seawater control
duration: 6 h larval exposure
challenge: transplantation of settled juveniles to 2 field sites in 2 seasons (winter and summer), with survival and growth followed for months
readouts: larval attachment rate; metamorphosis success; post-metamorphic colony survival; colony growth
effect_magnitude: Cu accelerated larval attachment in both seasons but inhibited metamorphosis; colony survival fell to about two-thirds of control in summer and to about 20% of control in winter; the survival decline occurred abruptly 3-5 weeks after exposure in summer and 14 weeks after exposure in winter, by which time colonies were 10-15 mm diameter (~100 zooids) and had undergone several budding cycles; surviving colonies grew more slowly than controls
replication: 2 seasons x 2 sites in SE Australia; transplanted colonies followed individually (n not extracted)
